items.summary: Carter said nothing about Weston in this interview; only the Hamilton archive's front-matter biography lists Weston among his early New York employers.
items.caution: The only Weston mention is the archive's biographical front matter ('found steady work in New York playing with Chico Hamilton, Randy Weston, and Eric Dolphy'), not Carter speaking. Do not attribute any line to Carter.
items.notes: relation 'played with' rests solely on the archive biography, not testimony; upstream 'in music group with' overstated it and cited the bio as Carter's words. Carter's 2020 Smithsonian interview is a separate witness item.

items.context: Riverside studio sessions before Monk; Cannonball Adderley's live album with 'High Fly'
items.one_liner: had him in the studio before monk
items.summary: Keepnews named Weston among the easygoing artists he had been in the studio with before Thelonious Monk, and said Cannonball Adderley's live album carried what he believed was the first recording of Weston's 'Hi-Fly'.
items.lead_quote: before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats.
items.second_quote: this was the first recording as far as I know of Randy Weston’s “High Fly” which of course has become quite a classic in its own right
items.caution: 'all pussycats' means easy to work with, set against Monk as 'a real tough cookie'; shown bare it can read as belittling. The second quote's claim that Cannonball's was the first recording of 'Hi-Fly' is Keepnews's own hedge ('as far as I know') and is probably wrong: Weston recorded the tune himself before Cannonball's 1959 live album (check discography before printing). 'High Fly' is the transcript's spelling of Hi-Fly. The 'waltz king' remark in the same block is Cannonball's on-record patter, reported, not Keepnews's judgement.
items.notes: A producer who recorded him: 'collaborated with' per spec. Upstream 'has met' understated it. Keepnews does not say in so many words that he produced Weston's records, only that he 'had been in the studio with' him.

items.one_liner: named him as a taller piano player
items.summary: McKenna, joking about being called a giant of the piano, offered Weston as a physically bigger pianist and passed on a story about him standing next to Wilt Chamberlain.
items.lead_quote: Yeah, but there’s bigger piano players, too. Remember Stan Kenton? How about Randy Weston?
items.second_quote: Did you hear about Randy Weston and some other tall piano player came in and happened to be standing next to Wilt Chamberlain, and that reduced everything.
items.caution: Both lines are a joke about height ('giant of the piano' taken literally); out of context 'bigger piano players' reads as a judgement of stature or talent. The Wilt Chamberlain story is hearsay ('Did you hear about').
items.notes: No contact stated.

items.context: Village clubs (Five Spot, Club Bohemia), from 1957
items.one_liner: went to the village when he worked there
items.summary: Ousley recalled going down to the Village clubs after arriving in New York in 1957, when Weston was working six nights a week, and named him as the kind of artist he interviewed on his public-access TV shows.
items.lead_quote: I would go down there at the time Randy Weston was down there and he worked, in fact they had music seven nights a week, I think Randy worked six
items.second_quote: doing interviews gives me an opportunity to do interviews with artists, say like Randy Weston, that people may go to hear but don’t get a chance to hear what they feel and what they think and what’s important to them.
items.caution: The second line ('say like Randy Weston') gives him as an example of the kind of artist Ousley interviews on cable TV; it does not state that Weston was ever actually on the show. The lead line ends mid-thought ('Randy worked six' nights a week).
items.notes: Upstream 'has met' is not stated in the testimony. The 1957 date comes from Ousley's next turn ('I came here in ’57').

items.one_liner: learned the publishing business from him
items.summary: Owens named Weston, after Donald Byrd, as one of his mentors and said Weston taught him how music publishing works, knowledge that led him into teaching the business of music.
items.lead_quote: Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works.
items.second_quote: mentors like Donald Byrd and Randy Weston helped me to understand the business side of music
items.notes: Input gives no QID for this Jimmy Owens (trumpeter); none invented. His Smithsonian interview is a separate witness item.

items.context: his band, about fifteen years to 1995; the Morocco film trip
items.one_liner: went to morocco to film his return
items.summary: Powell said fifteen years in Weston's band had been glorious, recalled the trip to Morocco to film his return there, and quoted him as wanting 'to put the magic back in music', calling him a spellbinder who leads by example and pays well.
items.lead_quote: he said, “I’m just trying to put the magic back in music.” And boy can he ever do it. He is a spellbinder.
items.second_quote: “What note goes here?” He’d say, “I don’t know, find a pretty one and play it.”
items.caution: In the Morocco story Powell runs the Gnawa together with the village he calls 'Joujouka' and names 'Brian Smith' of the Rolling Stones (Brian Jones); his dating of Weston's father's words and first Tangier visit ('maybe 25 years ago') is loose. Do not lift those details into captions. The title says Monk Rowe, but this first interview was conducted by Michael Woods.
items.notes: Framed Weston as the boss (joined his band, 'chosen by him', 'he pays very well', 'he won't hire you' if he cannot pay), hence 'played under'. Upstream 'played with' is right in substance. Other usable lines: 'I’ve been playing with Randy Weston for about the last 15 years, and it’s really been glorious' (216628); 'he’s just like Count Basie, I can’t say only better' (216650).

items.context: his group, late 1990s: Jamaica, Seville and European tours, the album Khepera
items.one_liner: toured europe with him while on dialysis
items.summary: Powell said every time Weston sat down at the piano it sounded like a concerto, called him the most scholarly person he knew, and told how his boss arranged his dialysis on European tours and offered to carry his bags.
items.lead_quote: It sounds like a concerto every time he sits down. It’s amazing.
items.second_quote: One of those mornings he knocked on my door at seven o’clock and said, “Benny, can I help you with your bags out?” I said, “Man, you’re the boss, I’m supposed to be helping you,” I said, “You don’t know how to be a boss man, you’re supposed to be tough.”
items.caution: The lead's 'he' needs Weston named beside it (the sentence before says 'I work with him now'). Powell's biographical asides (lives in Marrakesh and Brooklyn, 'working with the United Nations', 'living in Africa ... 30 years') are unverified and should not be lifted. 'the greatest pianist in the world' trails off into a self-correction about practising; do not quote it bare.
items.notes: He calls Weston 'the boss' and his 'employer', so 'played under' rather than upstream's 'collaborated with'. Other strong lines: 'He is the most scholarly person I know.' (216708); 'he’s like Duke Ellington. He can meld anything' (216713, starts with the fragment 'way,'); 'he comes across the Atlantic like it’s the crosstown bus' (216728).

items.one_liner: loved his pieces on “high flyin’”
items.summary: Ross named the Lambert, Hendricks & Ross album 'High Flyin’' among her favourites and said its Weston pieces were wonderful.
items.lead_quote: I loved “High Flyin’” which didn’t get that much distribution but it was a good album, and those things of Randy Weston’s are wonderful.
items.caution: 'those things of Randy Weston’s' is not specified; it means his compositions as sung on the LH&R album, and she names none. No contact with him is stated.

items.context: early sets with Gary Bartz in Baltimore
items.summary: Smith played a tune at the piano that Rowe named as Weston's 'Hi-Fly', and said only that they played things like that in his early Baltimore sets.
items.caution: The only words naming Weston ('Oh yeah, Randy Weston. “High Fly”?') are the interviewer's, not Smith's.
items.notes: He evidently knew the tune (he played it), which is the only basis for 'knows of'.

items.summary: Barron said nothing about Weston; the interviewer called a possible project with African instruments 'Randy Weston territory', and Barron assented and moved on to Hank Jones.
items.caution: 'Randy Weston territory.' is the interviewer's (Brown's) line, not Barron's.
items.notes: Barron's 'Yeah.' is the only assent.

items.one_liner: heard him on the jazzmobile in harlem
items.summary: DeJohnette said he used to go to hear Weston play at the Jazzmobile's flatbed-truck concerts in Harlem in the mid-1960s.
items.lead_quote: they used to bring flatbed trucks up into Harlem and they'd have concerts up there. I used to go hear Randy Weston play there.
items.notes: Audience member only; the anecdote moves at once to Idris Muhammad and Don Pullen.

items.context: the Five Spot, when the Jazztet was forming
items.one_liner: recalled his quartet at the five spot
items.summary: Fuller recalled that the Five Spot always booked two groups and that the first had been Weston and his quartet.
items.lead_quote: They always hire two groups at The Five Spot. First, it was Randy Weston and his quartet.
items.caution: The transcript is garbled here ('Jerry Mulligan', 'Danny Golson'); it is unclear whether Weston's quartet shared the bill with Fuller's group or was an earlier booking. No contact is stated.

items.context: New York, when Hendricks arrived on the scene; his lyric to 'Blues for Strayhorn'
items.one_liner: wrote a church-song lyric to his tune
items.summary: Hendricks said he admired and worked with Weston when he arrived on the scene, set his 'Blues for Strayhorn' as a church song, and placed him in a line of depth running from Duke Ellington through Monk.
items.lead_quote: Randy Weston also has depth, because he comes from Monk, which is the lineage Duke – Monk – Randy. So he has some of that depth.
items.second_quote: I liked Randy Weston. I worked with Randy at that time. Randy was very creative.
items.caution: 'some of that depth' ranks him just below Duke and Monk; the next sentence in the second block ('At that time he did all of what I consider his best tunes') implies his later work was weaker, so do not extend the second quote. Check that 'Blues for Strayhorn' is the title of a Weston composition before naming it. The interviewer, not Hendricks, mentions lyrics to Little Niles and Hi-Fly.
items.notes: 'I worked with Randy at that time' gives no detail of the work; 'collaborated with' rests on that plus writing a lyric to his tune.

items.one_liner: had his albums on the office wall
items.summary: Keepnews recalled Miles Davis seeing Weston's albums on the Riverside office wall and saying he was glad somebody had finally recorded him, then scorning the idea of recommending anyone to his own label boss.
items.lead_quote: he said, “Oh, Randy! I’m glad somebody got around to recording him. It should have been done along time ago,”
items.second_quote: We had some recent albums on the wall, including a couple of Randy Weston.
items.caution: The praise in the lead is Miles Davis's, reported by Keepnews; caption it as Miles's remark, not Keepnews's judgement. 'along time ago' is verbatim.
items.notes: The relation rests on the implication that Riverside recorded Weston (his albums on the office wall; Miles glad 'somebody got around to recording him'); Keepnews does not say here that he produced them. Upstream 'knows of' understates it. Do not carry in facts from his Hamilton interview.

items.context: CTI's Blue Moses; a CTI concert in Tangier
items.one_liner: first went to africa because of him
items.summary: Laws, reminded that he played on Weston's Blue Moses, said his first trip to Africa, to Tangier with CTI artists, came about because of Weston.
items.lead_quote: First time I went to Africa was because of Randy Weston.
items.second_quote: We all – when I say we, I’m talking about some of the CTI artists – went to Tangier.
items.caution: Laws only half-remembers playing on Blue Moses ('I played on that too, right?'; the interviewer confirms it) and did not know whether Weston lived in Tangier. The interviewer's warm tribute in 292074 is Brown's, not Laws's. The Weston passage follows directly on Laws's remarks about women and domestic disputes; do not show it with that context.
items.notes: Played on his record and a concert: 'played with' rather than upstream's 'collaborated with'.

items.context: his arranger, ’56 to ’96: Little Niles, Earth Birth, Pam’s Waltz
items.one_liner: wrote his arrangements for forty years
items.summary: Liston recalled meeting Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie, said she had arranged his music with complete freedom from ’56 to ’96, and thanked him for pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
items.lead_quote: I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.
items.second_quote: He brought Little Niles and all those things up to the house, and he said, “I think you should write these things for an album for me.” And I wrote them. I think it’s the best thing.
items.caution: 'because nobody else did' is her view after the stroke; in the next turn she names Frank and other arrangers as friends, so it should not be read as an accusation against named people. Many Weston lines in this interview are the interviewer Clora Bryant's ('Randy is your horn right now', the recording dates, 'in different clothing') and must not be attributed to Liston. '[Weston]' in 'Randy [Weston]' is the transcriber's bracket. 'He don’t tell me anything' (295901) means he gives her free rein, not that he is uncommunicative; do not show it without the freedom context.
items.notes: Follows the liston_build lead. Other strong lines of hers: 'Randy, I have all the freedom I want.' (295899); 'But we’ve been together – what? – ’56 to ’96. How many is that? 40 years.' (295901); 'He says I write like he writes.' (295903); 'He stayed over and met me when I finished the gig. He said, “I have to meet her.”' (295919); 'Randy pulled me out of the stroke, so I have to go with him.' (295937); 'Randy likes Thelonious much.' (296190). Venue of the meeting is hedged ('I guess Birdland'). 'Paul West' in 296214 is the session conductor, not Paul Weston.

items.context: Harlem and Brooklyn jam sessions, late 1940s; Max Roach's Brooklyn circle
items.one_liner: named him among the brooklyn players at sessions
items.summary: McLean named Weston among the Brooklyn musicians who came over to play at the Harlem jam sessions, and among the Brooklyn guys in Max Roach's circle.
items.lead_quote: So there were guys from Brooklyn that would come over and play. Randy Weston. We used to go to Brooklyn, to jam sessions over there.
items.notes: Both men were at the same jam sessions, but McLean does not say he played with or met Weston, so upstream 'has met' is not established. 301363 has only a bare 'Randy' in a roll-call of Brooklyn guys.

items.context: a left-wing union dance (c. 1947); the Jazz on Broadway concert series, 1964
items.one_liner: booked his large band for jazz on broadway
items.summary: Morgenstern recalled that one of the first live bands he ever saw, at a left-wing union dance, was Weston's with Ahmed Abdul-Malik on bass, and that his 1964 Jazz on Broadway series presented Weston with a fairly large band.
items.lead_quote: One of the first live bands I saw was at a left-wing union dance where Randy Weston had the band and Ahmed was the bass player.
items.second_quote: for which we did Lucky Thompson with an octet, and Randy Weston with a fairly large band
items.caution: The second quote is a fragment inside a run-on sentence. The 1947 date in the same sentence belongs to his first meeting Ahmed Abdul Malik; the union dance is only implied to be the same occasion. Weston is incidental in both passages (the stories are about Earl Hines and the concert series).
items.notes: 'collaborated with' rests on Morgenstern co-producing the concert series that presented Weston's band; he describes no personal dealings with him. Upstream 'has met' was based on the union dance, where he was only in the audience.

items.context: a musicians' organizing meeting on 135th Street; lessons in publishing
items.one_liner: got an inch-thick stack of his lead sheets
items.summary: Owens credited Weston, with Donald Byrd, for teaching him to keep his own publishing, and recalled Weston handing him an inch-thick stack of lead sheets at a musicians' meeting on 135th Street with the advice to write his music out if he wanted it recorded.
items.lead_quote: Randy Weston gave me a stack of about an inch of his lead sheets. One of the things he said was, “You’ve gotta have your stuff written out if you want people to record it.”
items.second_quote: I recall how Randy Weston and Donald Byrd, and talking to Horace Silver and Cannonball Adderley, and all of these musicians, Nat Adderley, how they gave me information freely.
items.notes: Upstream 'influenced by' is true but weaker than what he describes; 'mentor of' (Weston leading) fits. Input gives no QID for this Jimmy Owens; none invented. 308909 (Weston occasionally seen with a big band) and 308987 (a Jazzmobile student now playing saxophone with him) are passing mentions. Facts from his Hamilton interview are not carried over.

items.context: early New York career, after touring with Chico Hamilton; before or around Sonny Rollins
items.one_liner: for almost a year after chico hamilton’s tour
items.summary: Asked about working with Weston after returning from Chico Hamilton's tour, Carter said only that it lasted almost a year, 'plus', and that all those leaders brought something to his table.
items.caution: Carter's own words about Weston ('For almost a year.' / 'Plus.') sit in the interviewer's blocks' context, not in a block of his; his only block is the single word 'Randy.' There is no quotable line.
items.notes: The interviewer (Levy) raises Weston; Carter confirms the duration in his own words, which is enough for spoke_themselves=true but not for a quote. 'in music group with' (sideman among leaders Chico, Sonny, Randy) rather than upstream's 'collaborated with'.

items.context: both recording for Riverside; the early-1960s cultural trip to Africa
items.one_liner: recommended him for the africa trip
items.summary: Taylor recalled that he and Weston, both recording for Riverside, were fascinated by its African field recordings, that he recommended Weston for an early-1960s cultural trip to Africa when he could not go, and called him a remarkable musician who had gone back to the roots as few others had.
items.lead_quote: Randy Weston is a remarkable musician who has over the years taken the historical line from Africa that has been developed in the Americas and has done something very special with it.
items.second_quote: So I recommended Randy Weston and this is when Randy first went to Africa and he ultimately stayed there and did things.
items.caution: The second quote compresses history: 'this is when Randy first went to Africa and he ultimately stayed there' is Taylor's recollection; the trip and his later residence in Africa were years apart, and the claim that Taylor's recommendation sent him is Taylor's alone. In 317235 the transcript garbles the name as 'Randy Western' (Monk and 'Randy Western' as spare pianists); if that line is used, correct with [sic] or editorial note.
items.notes: 'friend of' on the strength of 'we used to talk about these things' and 'we talked about them a lot'; nothing stronger (no playing together) is stated. Input gives no QID for this Billy Taylor; none invented. Also usable: 'I mean he has gone back to the roots in way that few others have.' (verbatim 'in way').

items.one_liner: called him one of the spiritual leaders
items.summary: Oxenhorn named Weston with Sonny Rollins and Jimmy Heath as spiritual leaders.
items.lead_quote: Him, and Randy Weston and Jimmy Heath, these spiritual... They’re spiritual leaders, is what they are.
items.caution: 'Him' at the start of the quote is Sonny Rollins; the praise is shared among three men. She implies but does not state contact with them through the Jazz Foundation.

items.context: a jazz club near Tanglewood, summer before his last Berklee year
items.one_liner: took the club slot he was leaving
items.summary: LaBarbera recalled getting a summer gig at a jazz club near Tanglewood because Weston was leaving it.
items.caution: The club name is transcribed 'Avalock' (probably the Avaloch inn at Lenox); Weston is only the act whose departure opened the slot, as relayed by LaBarbera's brother.
items.notes: Input label 'Labarbera' fixed to 'Pat LaBarbera' from the doc's interviewee field. No contact stated, so upstream 'has met' is wrong. Nothing quotable about Weston himself.
